title: Stage 7: Middleware and an API key
summary: Meet the request pipeline: tag every response with a request id, then lock the tasks behind an API key.

steps.title: The request pipeline
body: Some jobs belong to *every* request, whatever the endpoint: logging it, timing it, checking who is calling. Copying that code into each handler would be tedious, and one day you would forget one.
ASP.NET Core has a place for such code. A request does not go straight to your endpoint. It travels through a **pipeline** of **middleware**, one after another, and the endpoint sits at the far end.
```text
request  ->  middleware A  ->  middleware B  ->  endpoint
response <-  middleware A  <-  middleware B  <-
Each middleware receives the request and a way to call the **next** step. That gives it three powers:
- do something **before** the rest runs (check a header, start a timer),
- do something **after** the rest has run (log the status code, stop the timer),
- **not call next at all** and answer the request itself. This is called short-circuiting, and it is how a request without permission is turned away before any endpoint sees it.
Because each middleware wraps everything after it, the order is like the layers of an onion: the first one in is the last one out.

steps.prompt: This console program has the shape of a pipeline: each step may do work before and after calling the next. What does it print?
steps.explain: `Outer` starts first and finishes last, because everything else happens inside its `await next()`. The request travels inward through the layers and the response travels back out through the same layers in reverse.

steps.title: Writing middleware with app.Use
body: The shortest way to add middleware is an inline lambda:
```csharp fragment
app.Use(async (context, next) =>
// before: the request is on its way in
await next(context);
// after: the endpoint has run

- `context` is the `HttpContext`: everything about this one request and its response. `context.Request` has the method, path, headers and query. `context.Response` has the status code, headers and body.
- `next` is the rest of the pipeline. `await next(context)` runs it.
Middleware runs in the order you add it with `app.Use`, and it runs for every request, including ones that end in a 404.
## Setting a response header
Headers are a dictionary on the response:
```csharp fragment
app.Use(async (context, next) =>
context.Response.Headers["X-Powered-By"] = "Dojo";
await next(context);

Set it **before** calling `next`. HTTP sends the status line and headers first and the body after them. Once the endpoint has started writing the body, the headers are already on their way and can no longer be changed.

Custom headers were traditionally given an `X-` prefix, and many well-known ones still have it. A common one is `X-Request-Id`: a unique id per request, sent back to the client and written to the logs. When a user reports a failed request, that id leads straight to the matching log lines.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines into a middleware that adds an `X-Request-Id` header to every response.
steps.explain: Make the id, put it on the response, then let the rest of the pipeline run. The header has to be set before `next`, while the response has not started.

steps.prompt: This middleware is meant to add a header to every response. Clients never receive it. Why?
options: By the time `next` returns, the endpoint has sent the response, headers first. It is too late to add one.
Middleware can read headers but only endpoints can set them.
Header names may not start with `X-`.
steps.explain: Headers travel ahead of the body. After `await next(context)` the endpoint has already written its response, so the headers are locked, and ASP.NET Core throws an exception on that line. Setting the header before `next` is the simple fix.

steps.title: Tag every response
prompt: Add a middleware that gives every response an `X-Request-Id` header.
- The value is a fresh id for each request. `Guid.NewGuid().ToString()` is fine. The tests only check that the header is there, is not empty, and differs between two requests.
- **Every** response carries it: successful ones, `400`s, `404`s from your endpoints, and the `404` for a URL that has no endpoint at all.
- Write it once, with `app.Use`. Do not touch the endpoints.
Everything else must behave as before.

static string Ids(JsonElement json) => json.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.Array

: "(not a JSON array)";
static JsonElement At(JsonElement json, int index) =>
json.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.Array && index < json.GetArrayLength() ? json[index] : default;
static async Task<string> IdsOf(HttpClient http, string url) => Ids(await DojoWeb.Json(await http.GetAsync(url)));
static bool HasError(JsonElement json) => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(DojoWeb.Prop(json, "error"));
static Task<HttpResponseMessage> Patch(HttpClient http, string url, object body) =>
http.PatchAsync(url, JsonContent.Create(body));
static string? RequestId(HttpResponseMessage response) =>
response.Headers.TryGetValues("X-Request-Id", out var values) ? string.Join(",", values) : null;

steps.title: Turning requests away
body: Right now anyone who can reach the server can delete every task. The simplest protection is an **API key**: a secret string that each client must send with every request.
The key travels in a **request header**:
```text
GET /tasks
X-Api-Key: dojo-secret
Not in the URL. URLs end up in browser history, server logs and proxy logs, and a secret in a URL leaks.
A request with no key, or a wrong one, gets **`401 Unauthorized`**: *I do not know who you are.*
Checking the key is a perfect job for middleware. It applies to many endpoints, and it must happen before any of them runs:
```csharp fragment
app.Use(async (context, next) =>
if (context.Request.Headers["X-Api-Key"] != "letmein")
context.Response.StatusCode = StatusCodes.Status401Unauthorized;
await context.Response.WriteAsJsonAsync(new { error = "API key required." });
return;
await next(context);

The `return` without calling `next` is the short-circuit. The endpoint never runs, so nothing is read and nothing is changed. Middleware does not return a result the way an endpoint does. You set the status code and write the body yourself, and `WriteAsJsonAsync` handles the JSON.
To protect only part of the API, look at the path:
```csharp fragment
if (context.Request.Path.StartsWithSegments("/admin")) { ... }
`StartsWithSegments("/admin")` is true for `/admin` and `/admin/users`, but not for `/administrator`. It compares whole path segments.
> **Tip:** `401` means *not identified*. Its sibling `403 Forbidden` means *I know who you are, and you may not do this*.

steps.prompt: The Tasks API now wants an API key for `/tasks`. Which status code fits each response?
items: `DELETE /tasks/2` with the right key, and task 2 exists
`GET /tasks/99` with the right key, and no task 99
`GET /tasks/99` with no key, and no task 99
`PUT /tasks/1` with the right key and a title of 300 characters
steps.explain: The key is checked before anything else, so a request without a valid key is always 401. It never gets far enough to learn whether task 99 exists, and that is deliberate: a stranger should not be able to probe your data.

steps.title: Configuration
body: A secret written into the source code is a problem. Everyone who can read the code can read the key, and changing it means changing the program.

Settings like this belong in **configuration**, which ASP.NET Core collects from several places: an `appsettings.json` file, environment variables, and command-line arguments. `builder.Configuration` gives you the merged result. Look a setting up by name:
```csharp fragment
var greeting = builder.Configuration["Greeting"] ?? "Hello";
The indexer returns `null` when the setting is not defined anywhere, so `??` supplies a default.

The same program can now run with different settings on your laptop and on a server, without a rebuild. In production the real key would be set in an environment variable, and the default in the code would only ever be used during development.
Read the value once, near the top of `Program.cs`, and let the middleware use the variable.

steps.prompt: No `appsettings.json` exists and no environment variable named `ApiKey` is set. What is `apiKey`?
steps.explain: A setting that is not defined comes back as `null`, not as an exception, and `??` replaces that `null` with the default. If an environment variable `ApiKey` were set, its value would win.

steps.title: Require an API key
prompt: Protect the tasks with an API key.
- Read the expected key from configuration, with a default: `builder.Configuration["ApiKey"] ?? "dojo-secret"`. The tests run with nothing configured, so the key they send is `dojo-secret`.
- Every request whose path is `/tasks` or starts with `/tasks/` must carry the header `X-Api-Key` with exactly that value. All methods: `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`.
- A missing or wrong key gets `401 Unauthorized` with a JSON body `{"error":"..."}`, and the endpoint does not run. Nothing is created, changed or deleted.
- `GET /health` and `GET /` stay public: no key needed.
- Do it in one middleware, added **after** the request-id middleware, so that a `401` response carries an `X-Request-Id` header too.
With the right key, everything behaves as before.

static string? RequestId(HttpResponseMessage response) =>
response.Headers.TryGetValues("X-Request-Id", out var values) ? string.Join(",", values) : null;
static void HasRequestId(string what, HttpResponseMessage response) =>
